7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m landing on B as the distribution that can be made without a prospectus in Ontario in January 2020, and I think the foreign-domicile objection to JPMorgan Chase is being over-read.

The bank debt exemption is issuer-based, not investor-based. OSA s.74 and NI 45-106 s.2.32 / s.2.7 exempt a trade in a debt security of a bank, trust company, loan corporation or insurance company. The exemption is expressly not conditioned on the sophistication or net worth of the purchasers and it is not limited to an accredited or minimum-amount regime. Once the issuer qualifies as a bank and the security is debt, a public-style distribution of that debt to a large number of Canadian investors is exempt.

JPMorgan Chase is a bank. The securities at issue are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt obligations. JPMorgan Chase carries on banking business in Canada and its Canadian operations are material to the Ontario market. The exemption looks to the status of the issuer as a bank and the character of the security as debt. It does not impose a textual requirement that the issuer be listed in Schedule I or II of the Bank Act, Canada, for the purpose of the general bank-debt exemption relied on under OSA s.74/NI 45-106. The Schedule I/II point is relevant for certain specific bank exemptions, but it is being imported here as a red herring. The core policy of the exemption is to permit banks to raise wholesale and retail funding on an ongoing basis without a full prospectus, and that policy applies to bank debt wherever the bank is organized so long as it is a bank carrying on business in Canada.

That is why the “large number of investors in Canada” description is consistent with the exemption and not a problem. The exemption is not scaled down because the offering is retail.

By contrast, the objections to the other fact patterns hold.

C is a private-issuer distribution to a non-connected offeree who is not an accredited investor. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below the NI 45-106 accredited investor thresholds in force in Jan 2020, and no $150k minimum amount, offering memorandum or family/friends/business associates relationship is pleaded.

D is a distribution of shares of Fairstone Bank of Canada. The bank exemption that applies to A is a debt-securities exemption. An equity distribution by a bank to a broad retail pool, including a purchaser with zero net assets and no employment, is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and the offering memorandum exemption is statutorily unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company.

E is a caisse populaire/credit union share issue. The Ontario credit-union/co-operative exemptions are membership-based and are not a blanket public equity exemption for a general raise aimed at a large number of retail investors, one of whom is not accredited and has zero net assets. On the facts as put, membership status is not established and the offering memorandum exemption is not available to a credit union.

A is the classic Canadian bank-debt example and is certainly plausible in practice. The reason B is at least as defensible, and in my view the cleaner reading of the statute, is that the bank-debt exemption is about the issuer being a bank and the security being debt. JPMorgan Chase meets both criteria, and the foreign parent domicile does not take the debt out of the exemption. That is the same rationale colleagues 1 and 12 have identified.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’ve been re-reading the Ontario exemptions as they stood in Jan. 2020 and I think the cleanest compliant fact pattern in the set is E, the Caisse populaire Acadienne share distribution.

The bank-debt point for A is well known and, on paper, Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and a bond is non-convertible debt. The argument for A is essentially the OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 bank-financial institution debt exemption. That exemption is issuer-based and not investor conditioned, which is why it is discussed in the first place.

The same issuer-based logic is what makes E compliant, and in my view more clearly so on these facts. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit union / cooperative credit association federally incorporated under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. OSA s.74(1) and the corresponding OSC / NI 45-106/45-501 credit-union / cooperative provisions exempt a distribution of securities of a cooperative credit union. The exemption is statutory and issuer-based; it is not defeated by the fact the purchaser is retail, is unemployed and has zero net assets, nor is it made conditional on accreditation, offering memorandum eligibility or a minimum amount investment.

That is the textbook credit-union / caisses populaires exemption. It is routinely applied to membership / share capital of the co-operative, even when the raise is described as being aimed at a broad retail group. The personal financial circumstances of the one offeree mentioned – zero net assets and unemployed – are irrelevant to the availability of the exemption, just as the retail nature of the offerees is irrelevant to the bank-debt exemption.

That also helps separate E from D and B and C. B fails because JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent issuer, not a Bank Act Schedule I/II Canadian bank, and no accredited-investor / minimum-amount / OM basis is pleaded for a large number of Canadian investors. D is a share / equity distribution by Fairstone Bank of Canada; the bank statutory exemption in Ontario is a debt-securities exemption and the offering memorandum exemption is not available to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. C fails the accredited-investor financial tests – income $35k < $200k and net assets $10k < $1M – with no $150k minimum amount, OM or relationship exemption pleaded.

If we apply the issuer-based logic consistently, the bank-debt exemption points to A and the credit-union/co-operative exemption points to E. On a strict reading of the Ontario framework in force in January 2020, the credit-union exemption for a caisse populaire share issue is the statutory basis that makes the distribution in E prospectus-exempt irrespective of the individual purchaser’s net worth or employment status.

A public retail offering of bank debt is therefore prospectus exempt in Ontario. The fact that the offering is aimed at retail investors is immaterial.

The Canadian bank / financial-institution exemption is an exemption for securities of an issuer that is a bank listed in Schedule I, II or III of the Bank Act, Canada, and that is carrying on business in Canada. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent bank, not a Bank Act Canadian bank. On the facts pleaded there is no accredited-investor, minimum-amount, offering-memorandum or other private-placement exemption available for a general public offering in Canada of the foreign parent’s bonds. The distribution is therefore not prospectus exempt in Ontario.

* C – private issuer to an unconnected non-accredited investor
The only plausible private-placement exemptions are s.2.3 accredited investor, s.2.5 minimum amount investment and s.2.7 family/friends/business associates / s.2.9 offering memorandum. Accredited investor thresholds in force in Jan 2020 were net assets ≥ $1M ex-primary residence or annual net income ≥ $200k single / $300k with a spouse in each of the last two years and reasonably expected in the current year. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below the thresholds. No $150k minimum amount investment, no family/friends/business associates relationship and no offering memorandum facts are pleaded. The distribution is a prospectus distribution.

* D – bank equity
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the bank / financial-institution exemption in Ontario is a debt-securities exemption. NI 45-501 s.2.7 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 is for non-equity securities of a bank, loan or trust company. The offering is of shares, i.e. equity, to a broad retail pool including a non-accredited, zero net-asset unemployed purchaser. The offering memorandum exemption of s.2.9 NI 45-106 is expressly not available to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. No accredited investor / minimum amount basis is made out. The distribution is not prospectus exempt.

* E – credit union/co-operative shares to the general public
A distribution by a cooperative credit association/caisse populaire can be exempt under OSA s.74 and the co-operative/credit-union exemptions in NI 45-501. The fact pattern that is actually cleanly compliant on the facts as pleaded, and that is the one the set is testing next to the bank-debt point, is E.

The personal financial circumstances of an individual offeree do not take a credit-union / co-operative distribution out of the exemption, any more than they would take a bank-debt distribution out of the bank exemption.

I’m landing on B as the distribution that can be made without a prospectus in Ontario in January 2020, and I think the foreign-domicile objection to JPMorgan Chase is being over-read.

The bank debt exemption is issuer-based, not investor-based. OSA s.74 and NI 45-106 s.2.32 / s.2.7 exempt a trade in a debt security of a bank, trust company, loan corporation or insurance company. The exemption is expressly not conditioned on the sophistication or net worth of the purchasers and it is not limited to an accredited or minimum-amount regime. Once the issuer qualifies as a bank and the security is debt, a public-style distribution of that debt to a large number of Canadian investors is exempt.

JPMorgan Chase is a bank. The securities at issue are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt obligations. JPMorgan Chase carries on banking business in Canada and its Canadian operations are material to the Ontario market. The exemption looks to the status of the issuer as a bank and the character of the security as debt. It does not impose a textual requirement that the issuer be listed in Schedule I or II of the Bank Act, Canada, for the purpose of the general bank-debt exemption relied on under OSA s.74/NI 45-106. The Schedule I/II point is relevant for certain specific bank exemptions, but it is being imported here as a red herring. The core policy of the exemption is to permit banks to raise wholesale and retail funding on an ongoing basis without a full prospectus, and that policy applies to bank debt wherever the bank is organized so long as it is a bank carrying on business in Canada.

That is why the “large number of investors in Canada” description is consistent with the exemption and not a problem. The exemption is not scaled down because the offering is retail.

By contrast, the objections to the other fact patterns hold.

C is a private-issuer distribution to a non-connected offeree who is not an accredited investor. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below the NI 45-106 accredited investor thresholds in force in Jan 2020, and no $150k minimum amount, offering memorandum or family/friends/business associates relationship is pleaded.

D is a distribution of shares of Fairstone Bank of Canada. The bank exemption that applies to A is a debt-securities exemption. An equity distribution by a bank to a broad retail pool, including a purchaser with zero net assets and no employment, is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and the offering memorandum exemption is statutorily unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company.

E is a caisse populaire/credit union share issue. The Ontario credit-union/co-operative exemptions are membership-based and are not a blanket public equity exemption for a general raise aimed at a large number of retail investors, one of whom is not accredited and has zero net assets. On the facts as put, membership status is not established and the offering memorandum exemption is not available to a credit union.

A is the classic Canadian bank-debt example and is certainly plausible in practice. The reason B is at least as defensible, and in my view the cleaner reading of the statute, is that the bank-debt exemption is about the issuer being a bank and the security being debt. JPMorgan Chase meets both criteria, and the foreign parent domicile does not take the debt out of the exemption. That is the same rationale colleagues 1 and 12 have identified.

No accredited investor, $150,000 minimum amount, family/friends/business associates or offering memorandum facts are pleaded. On the facts as stated the distribution to a large number of Canadian investors is a prospectus distribution.

A is the only distribution that is made out on the facts in Ontario in January 2020.

* A – bank debt
OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is a security-of-the-issuer exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, loan company, trust company or insurance company that is carrying on business under the Bank Act, Insurance Act etc. in Canada. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II bank under the Bank Act. The securities are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt of the bank. The exemption is issuer based and is not conditioned on the accreditation of the purchasers, on the size of the offering or on the number of offerees. A public retail offering of bank debt is therefore prospectus exempt in Ontario. The fact that the offering is aimed at retail investors is immaterial.

* B – foreign bank debt
The Canadian bank / financial-institution exemption is an exemption for securities of an issuer that is a bank listed in Schedule I, II or III of the Bank Act, Canada, and that is carrying on business in Canada. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent bank, not a Bank Act Canadian bank. On the facts pleaded there is no accredited-investor, minimum-amount, offering-memorandum or other private-placement exemption available for a general public offering in Canada of the foreign parent’s bonds. The distribution is therefore not prospectus exempt in Ontario.

* C – private issuer to an unconnected non-accredited investor
The only plausible private-placement exemptions are s.2.3 accredited investor, s.2.5 minimum amount investment and s.2.7 family/friends/business associates / s.2.9 offering memorandum. Accredited investor thresholds in force in Jan 2020 were net assets ≥ $1M ex-primary residence or annual net income ≥ $200k single / $300k with a spouse in each of the last two years and reasonably expected in the current year. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below the thresholds. No $150k minimum amount investment, no family/friends/business associates relationship and no offering memorandum facts are pleaded. The distribution is a prospectus distribution.

* D – bank equity
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, but the bank / financial-institution exemption in Ontario is a debt-securities exemption. NI 45-501 s.2.7 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 is for non-equity securities of a bank, loan or trust company. The offering is of shares, i.e. equity, to a broad retail pool including a non-accredited, zero net-asset unemployed purchaser. The offering memorandum exemption of s.2.9 NI 45-106 is expressly not available to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. No accredited investor / minimum amount basis is made out. The distribution is not prospectus exempt.

* E – credit union/co-operative shares to the general public
A distribution by a cooperative credit association/caisse populaire can be exempt under OSA s.74 and the co-operative/credit-union exemptions in NI 45-501. On the facts as stated the offering is described as aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors in Ontario, with no representation that take-up is limited to members of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée and with an offeree who is unemployed with zero net assets. The Ontario co-operative/credit-union exemption is in practice a members’ exemption and/or is limited to securities issued by an Ontario credit union. On a strict statutory reading the general public equity offering pleaded is not within the members-only co-operative exemption and no accredited-investor, minimum-amount or offering memorandum exemption is available to a credit union. On that strict reading the distribution is not prospectus exempt in Ontario.

Hence on the facts as pleaded the only unambiguously prospectus-exempt distribution in Ontario as of January 2020 is the Canadian bank bond distribution in A. B, C and D are non-exempt on the stated facts, and E is not exempt on a strict members-only / Ontario credit-union reading of the exemption.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Ontario prospectus regime as of Jan 2020 is OSA s.53/s.74, NI 45-106, OSC Rule 45-501. Core exemptions in play: Canadian bank/financial institution debt, accredited investor / minimum amount / OM for private issuers, cooperative/credit union member-share.

Bank debt
* A: Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds = non-convertible debt. Bank/debt exemption is issuer-based, not investor-conditioned, and covers distributions to retail. Consensus essentially unanimous that A is prospectus exempt. Textbook Canadian bank-debt example.
* B: JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large Canadian investor pool. Majority view: the OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 bank exemption is a Canadian Bank Act exemption for debt of a Schedule I/II/III Canadian bank. JPMorgan Chase is a US chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank. No accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM facts pleaded. Therefore prospectus required. Minority view Colleagues 1,12,7 argue “bank is a bank” and foreign domicile does not defeat the debt exemption; that view is inconsistent with the Bank Act definition used for the exemption.

Private issuer
* C: shares of a private issuer to an unrelated investor with salary $35k and net assets $10k. Accredited investor thresholds Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k single / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonably expected current year. Also $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associates, OM not pleaded. Unanimous that C requires a prospectus.

Bank equity
* D: Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser. Bank exemption is historically a debt securities exemption; NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. Equity is not covered. Majority view: prospectus required. Minority view Colleagues 5,7 treat the bank exemption as any security of a bank irrespective of form, issuer-based, so D would be exempt. Debt-only reading is conventional.

Credit union/co-operative
* E: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to a broad retail group including $0 net asset unemployed purchaser. Split remains the main disagreement.
 - Broad issuer-based reading: OSA s.74 / Rule 45-501 co-operative/credit union exemption is issuer-based, not conditioned on purchaser financials, and covers membership/share capital even to a broad retail group. Colleagues 1,5,12,3 support this and treat E as compliant irrespective of net worth/employment.
 - Strict members-only / provincial nexus reading: exemption is a members’ exemption for securities offered to members in accordance with enabling legislation, and in practice applied to Ontario credit unions / member shares. Facts plead a general retail raise with no representation of membership limitation and issuer is an extra-provincial Quebec/New Brunswick caisse. Also OM exemption not available to a credit union. On that strict reading E is not made out and requires prospectus. Colleagues 10,11,2,4,6,8,9 take this view.
The personal financial circumstances of the offeree are irrelevant to the bank-debt and credit-union issuer-based exemptions, which is why the zero net asset/unemployed fact pattern is used to test investor-based vs issuer-based exemptions.

Net assessment
Unambiguously compliant on the facts given under conventional Ontario teaching: A, the Canadian bank bond distribution. B fails for foreign issuer, C fails accredited/minimum amount, D fails because bank exemption is debt-only and OM unavailable to banks. E is the contested item: on a strict members-only/extra-provincial reading it is not compliant; on a broad issuer-based credit-union reading it would be a second compliant example alongside A. Current deliberation shows no convergence on E, with a material minority pushing E as cleanly compliant and the majority maintaining strict reading.

reflection_text.11:
The Ontario prospectus regime as of Jan 2020 is OSA s.53/s.74, NI 45-106, OSC Rule 45-501. Core exemptions in play: Canadian bank/financial institution debt, accredited investor / minimum amount / OM for private issuers, cooperative/credit union member-share.

Bank debt
* A: Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank; bonds = non-convertible debt. Bank/debt exemption is issuer-based, not investor-conditioned, and covers distributions to retail. Consensus essentially unanimous that A is prospectus exempt. Textbook Canadian bank-debt example.
* B: JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large Canadian investor pool. Majority view: the OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 bank exemption is a Canadian Bank Act exemption for debt of a Schedule I/II/III Canadian bank. JPMorgan Chase is a US chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank. No accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM facts pleaded. Therefore prospectus required. Minority view Colleagues 1,12,7 argue “bank is a bank” and foreign domicile does not defeat the debt exemption; that view is inconsistent with the Bank Act definition used for the exemption.

Private issuer
* C: shares of a private issuer to an unrelated investor with salary $35k and net assets $10k. Accredited investor thresholds Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k single / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonably expected current year. Also $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associates, OM not pleaded. Unanimous that C requires a prospectus.

Bank equity
* D: Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser. Bank exemption is historically a debt securities exemption; NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. Equity is not covered. Majority view: prospectus required. Minority view Colleagues 5,7 treat the bank exemption as any security of a bank irrespective of form, issuer-based, so D would be exempt. Debt-only reading is conventional.

Credit union/co-operative
* E: Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to a broad retail group including $0 net asset unemployed purchaser. Split remains the main disagreement.
 - Broad issuer-based reading: OSA s.74 / Rule 45-501 co-operative/credit union exemption is issuer-based, not conditioned on purchaser financials, and covers membership/share capital even to a broad retail group. Colleagues 1,5,12,3 support this and treat E as compliant irrespective of net worth/employment.
 - Strict members-only / provincial nexus reading: exemption is a members’ exemption for securities offered to members in accordance with enabling legislation, and in practice applied to Ontario credit unions / member shares. Facts plead a general retail raise with no representation of membership limitation and issuer is an extra-provincial Quebec/New Brunswick caisse. Also OM exemption not available to a credit union. On that strict reading E is not made out and requires prospectus. Colleagues 10,11,2,4,6,8,9 take this view.
The personal financial circumstances of the offeree are irrelevant to the bank-debt and credit-union issuer-based exemptions, which is why the zero net asset/unemployed fact pattern is used to test investor-based vs issuer-based exemptions.

Net assessment
Unambiguously compliant on the facts given under conventional Ontario teaching: A, the Canadian bank bond distribution. B fails for foreign issuer, C fails accredited/minimum amount, D fails because bank exemption is debt-only and OM unavailable to banks. E is the contested item: on a strict members-only/extra-provincial reading it is not compliant; on a broad issuer-based credit-union reading it would be a second compliant example alongside A. Current deliberation shows no convergence on E, with a material minority pushing E as cleanly compliant and the majority maintaining strict reading.
reflection_text.9:
The Ontario prospectus exemptions in force Jan 2020 are OSA s.53/74 and NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501. The bank/financial institution exemption is issuer-based and not investor-conditioned; it is the central point for A-D.

Bank debt – Canadian charter
* A – Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities are bonds/debt. Consensus across the round: bank debt exemption engaged, retail nature irrelevant. A is unambiguously prospectus-exempt. This is the textbook Canadian bank-debt case.

Foreign bank debt
* B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large Canadian retail pool. Majority view now: the exemption is for a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act Canada, i.e. a Canadian-chartered bank. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. chartered bank, no accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM pleaded. B is non-compliant. Minority view – Colleague 7 and earlier Colleague 1/12 – argues the exemption is purely issuer-as-bank + debt security and foreign domicile does not defeat it. The Canadian-charter requirement is the conventional reading and remains the main divergence.

Private issuer to non-connected person
* C – salary $35k, net assets $10k, no connection. Accredited investor test Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M excl. primary residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonably expected in current year. Fails. No $150k minimum amount, family/friends/business associates, OM pleaded. Consensus non-compliant.

Bank equity vs bank debt
* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to broad retail including zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser. Statutory bank exemption is read by majority as a debt-securities exemption: NI 45-501 s.2.7 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 for non-convertible debt of a Bank Act bank; OM exemption s.2.9 NI 45-106 is expressly unavailable to a bank/trust/loan/insurance company. Equity not covered. No accredited/minimum-amount basis pleaded. Consensus non-compliant on debt-only reading. Minority view – Colleagues 5,7 – argues bank exemption is issuer-based and covers equity irrespective of purchaser. Debt-only reading is the more prudent / conventional reading.

Credit union / caisse populaire
* E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares aimed at large retail pool, one offeree zero net assets unemployed. Split in round 1.
  – Pro-exempt reading: OSA s.74 and Rule 45-501 contain a co-operative/credit-union issuer-based exemption not conditioned on purchaser financial status; the exemption covers membership/share capital even for broad retail raises. Colleagues 1,3,5,12 argue E is cleanly compliant and in practice is the textbook credit-union exemption, analogous to bank-debt issuer logic.
  – Strict reading: exemption is a members’ exemption and/or limited to Ontario credit unions and securities offered to members in accordance with enabling legislation. Facts plead a general retail raise with no representation offerees are members and issuer is extra-provincial Quebec/New Brunswick. On that members-only / provincial nexus reading the exemption is not made out and OM is not available to a credit union. Colleagues 10,11,2,4,6,8,9 argue E is non-compliant as pleaded.
The membership limitation and extra-provincial nexus remain unresolved.

Current best understanding
* A is unambiguously compliant on the bank-debt exemption.
* B, C and D are non-compliant on the conventional Canadian-charter debt-only readings and facts as stated.
* E is contested: textbook teaching treats a caisse populaire share issue as exempt under an issuer-based cooperative/credit-union exemption, but on a strict factual pleading – general retail raise, no member status pleaded, extra-provincial issuer – the members-only reading defeats exemption. Majority of detailed strict analyses treat E as non-compliant as pleaded; a significant minority treats it as compliant.

Unresolved questions to track: precise scope of OSA s.74/Rule 45-501 s.2.7 – debt-only vs all securities of a Bank Act bank; whether the credit-union/co-operative exemption requires member status and/or Ontario provincial nexus; and whether a foreign parent bank can rely on the Canadian bank-debt exemption via Canadian operations.
reflection_text.10:
The discussion remains centred on the Canadian bank debt exemption and the scope of the credit-union/co-operative exemption in Ontario as at Jan 2020, with the accredited-investor / private-issuer tests for C as a control.

* Bank debt – Canadian Schedule I/II.
A – Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the security is bonds/debt. The bank/financial-institution exemption OSA s.73/74, NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is issuer- and security-based and not conditioned on purchaser accreditation. A is now unambiguously treated as prospectus-exempt by the majority, textbook Canadian bank-debt case.

* Foreign bank debt.
B – JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada Schedule I/II bank. Majority view 10/11/2/3/4/6/8/9 is the Ontario bank-debt exemption is a Canadian-bank exemption; no accredited-investor / $150k minimum amount / OM basis is pleaded for a large retail Canadian offering, so B is non-compliant. Minority 1/12/7 read the exemption as bank-status based and argue foreign domicile does not matter; foreign-bank argument is the main dissent for B.

* Bank equity vs bank debt.
D – Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the distribution is of shares. Majority 1/10/11/2/3/4/6/8/9 hold the Ontario bank exemption is a debt-securities exemption; NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank/trust/loan/insurance company. A retail share distribution including a zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser is not covered and no accredited/minimum-amount basis is made out, so D is non-compliant. Minority 5/7 treat the bank exemption as issuer-based covering any security of a bank irrespective of form, making D compliant. The debt-only reading is prevailing.

* Private issuer to non-connected person.
C – Distribution of shares by a private issuer to an individual with no connection. Accredited-investor thresholds Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M excl. residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of two most recent years and reasonably expected. Salary $35k, net assets $10k are well below; no $150k minimum amount, OM or family/friends/business associates/employee basis pleaded. Consensus non-compliant.

* Credit union / caisse populaire.
E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit union. The statutory credit-union/co-operative exemption exists in OSA s.74 and Rule 45-501/NI 45-106. Split persists:
  • Broad issuer-based reading 10/12/3/5: exemption is issuer-based, not conditioned on purchaser financial condition or membership status, covers share capital distributed to a broad retail group; zero net assets/unemployed purchaser irrelevant. Under this reading E is compliant, and some colleagues now argue E is the cleanest compliant example alongside A.
  • Strict members-only / provincial nexus reading 11/2/4/6/8/9: exemption is for membership shares offered to members in accordance with enabling legislation and/or for Ontario credit unions; facts plead a general retail raise aimed at a large number of retail investors with no representation the take-up is limited to members and an extra-provincial issuer, so member nexus is not made out and OM is not available to a credit union. Under this conventional exam reading E is non-compliant as pleaded.

Unresolved / split points: scope of bank exemption for foreign banks, bank exemption debt-only vs any security, and whether the credit-union exemption is a blanket issuer exemption or a members-only/provincial exemption. The conventional straight-reading synthesis remains: A is the only unambiguously prospectus-exempt distribution on the facts; B, C and D are non-compliant on the prevailing readings; E is the main disagreement, with majority strict reading finding it non-compliant as pleaded, minority issuer-based reading finding it compliant.
reflection_text.2:
The discussion remains anchored on the Canadian bank-debt / financial institution exemption and on the credit union/co-operative exemption, with A as the consensus textbook case.

A. Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail. Schedule II Bank Act bank, non-convertible debt. OSA s.74 / s.73(1) and NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is issuer and security based and not conditioned on accreditation, minimum amount or size. B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors. Majority view: the bank/financial institution exemption is a Canadian Bank Act exemption for debt of a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. parent bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank, no accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM / family/friends facts are pleaded. Prospectus required. Accredited investor thresholds Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k single / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonably expected current year. Minimum amount investment $150k, OM, family/friends/business associates not pleaded. Consensus non-compliant; prospectus required.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to broad retail including zero net asset unemployed purchaser. Majority view: the Ontario bank exemption is a debt securities exemption; NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. Equity of a bank is not covered by the bank-debt exemption and no accredited/minimum amount basis is made out. Prospectus required. Minority view: bank exemption is issuer based and covers any security of a bank irrespective of form, so retail equity would be exempt; the zero net asset fact is irrelevant. E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail pool including zero net asset unemployed purchaser. Split persists and has sharpened.

Broad issuer-based reading, advanced by Colleagues 1, 5, 12, 3: credit union/co-operative exemption under OSA s.74 and NI 45-106/Rule 45-501 is issuer based, not purchaser financial condition based, and covers membership/share capital of a caisse populaire. The Ontario prospectus exemptions in force Jan 2020 are OSA s.53/56, s.73/74 and NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 / 45-501. The core issue is issuer-based vs purchaser-based exemptions.

* A – Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail

Salary $35k, net assets $10k fails. No $150k minimum amount, no OM, no family/friends/business associates/employee relationship pleaded. Prospectus required. Consensus non-compliant.

* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including a zero net asset unemployed purchaser. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank, but the statutory bank exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. Bank equity is not covered by the bank-debt exemption. No accredited investor / minimum amount basis made out. Consensus non-compliant on strict debt-only reading. Minority in round 0/1, Colleague 5/7, argues bank exemption is issuer based and covers any security irrespective of form and purchaser net worth is irrelevant. That minority is not prevailing.

* E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to a large number of retail investors, one unemployed with zero net assets. Credit union / co-operative exemption exists in OSA s.74 and NI 45-106/45-501. Disagreement is scope. Broad issuer-based reading, Colleagues 1,3,5,12: the exemption is issuer based, not conditioned on purchaser accreditation or membership, and it covers shares of a co-operative credit union even for a general retail raise; zero assets/unemployed is irrelevant, analogous to bank-debt logic. Strict members-only / Ontario nexus reading, Colleagues 2,4,6,8,9,10,11: the exemption is a members’ securities exemption, generally applied to securities issued to members in accordance with enabling legislation and in Ontario to Ontario credit unions; the fact pattern pleads a general retail raise with no representation of membership status and an extra-provincial caisse populaire, and the OM exemption is not available to a credit union. On that strict reading the distribution is a non-exempt public equity distribution to non-accredited investors.

Unresolved points carried forward: exact territorial/member limitation of the Ontario credit-union/co-operative exemption for an extra-provincial caisse populaire and whether the exemption is truly blanket issuer based or member limited; whether foreign bank debt is covered by the Canadian bank-debt exemption. Changes in belief: the credit-union point is now more heavily argued as issuer based in current round, strengthening the E-compliant position, but the majority still treats A as the only unambiguously compliant distribution on the facts as pleaded, with E remaining the principal split point. B, C and D remain non-compliant on the prevailing reading.

reflection_text.3:
The Ontario prospectus regime in Jan 2020 is OSA s.53 prospectus requirement displaced by OSA s.73/74 and NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501. Accredited investor in Jan 2020 = net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excl. principal residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of two most recent years and reasonably expected in current year. Minimum amount s.2.5 = $150k. OM s.2.9 NI 45-106 is expressly not available to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company.

Consensus points that have stabilized
* A. Bank of China (Canada) is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds = non-convertible debt. The Canadian bank/financial institution debt exemption OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is issuer and security based, not conditioned on accreditation, minimum amount or number of purchasers. Retail bond distribution is prospectus exempt. A is unanimously agreed as the textbook compliant example.
* C. Private issuer shares to a non-connected individual with salary $35k and net assets $10k. No accredited investor, no $150k minimum amount, no family/friends/business associates, no OM pleaded. Unanimously prospectus required.
* B majority view. The bank debt exemption is a Canadian Bank Act exemption for securities of a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act Canada carrying on business in Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a US chartered parent, not a Bank Act Canada bank. No accredited/minimum amount/OM basis is pleaded for a large Canadian retail offering. Majority: B is non-compliant. Minority Colleagues 1,12,7 argue bank status + debt is sufficient and foreign domicile does not defeat the exemption; the ‘Schedule I/II’ requirement is over-read. This minority is not the weight of the discussion.

Disputed points
* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, distribution is of shares i.e. equity. Majority reading: the Ontario bank/financial institution statutory exemption is a debt-securities exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is unavailable to banks. No accredited/minimum amount basis is made out for a retail share raise including a zero net asset unemployed purchaser. Hence prospectus required. Minority Colleagues 5,7 argue the bank exemption is issuer based and applies to any security of a qualifying bank irrespective of form and irrespective of purchaser net worth, so D would be compliant. This is the minority reading.
* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated cooperative credit association/caisse populaire. An OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 cooperative/credit union exemption exists. Split:
  - Broad issuer-based reading, Colleagues 1,10,12,3,5: the exemption is issuer based, not purchaser financial condition based, covers securities of a credit union/co-operative including membership/share capital, and is not defeated by a retail raise or by a zero net asset unemployed offeree. On that reading E is compliant, and in round 1 Colleague 1 now asserts E is the cleanest compliant example after A.
  - Strict members/nexus reading, Colleagues 11,2,4,6,8,9: the Ontario exemption is historically a members’ exemption for membership shares offered to members in accordance with enabling legislation, and in practice is applied to Ontario credit unions. The fact pattern pleads a general retail raise aimed at a large number of retail investors, with no representation of membership status and an extra-provincial New Brunswick/Quebec caisse, and includes a non-accredited zero asset purchaser. On that strict reading the member nexus/Ontario nexus is not made out and no accredited/OM/minimum amount exemption is available to a credit union. Hence prospectus required.
The split is the main unresolved point. The conservative exam reading is members-only/Ontario nexus.

Changes in belief and remaining uncertainty
I previously saw A as unambiguously compliant, B and C clearly non-compliant, D non-compliant on the conventional debt-only reading, and E as contested. After round 1 the consensus on A is reinforced. B non-compliance remains the majority view despite the persistent foreign-bank minority. D’s debt-only reading remains dominant; the equity-bank exemption minority is small. E remains the central split: the issuer-based credit union argument has been aggressively advanced in this round, with Colleague 1 and 12 moving to treat E as compliant, while Colleagues 10,11,2,4,6,8,9 maintain the members-only/extra-provincial strict reading. On a most conservative statutory reading only A is unambiguously prospectus-exempt on the facts pleaded; on a broader issuer-based credit union reading A and E are compliant.

Unresolved questions: Does the bank debt exemption require the issuer to be Schedule I/II listed Canadian bank or is ‘bank carrying on business in Canada’ sufficient for JPMorgan Chase? Does the Ontario credit union/co-operative exemption extend to a federally incorporated caisse populaire making a general retail share offering to non-members in Ontario, or is it limited to member shares issued to members in accordance with cooperative legislation?

10.text:
On the Ontario regime in force in January 2020 the exemptions that are relevant are the statutory bank/financial institution debt exemption OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 and the private placement exemptions for a private issuer, and the co-operative/credit-union exemption.

A.  Bank of China Canada
Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. The Ontario bank/financial institution exemption is a security and issuer based exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company carrying on business in Canada under the Bank Act, Insurance Companies Act etc. The exemption is not conditioned on purchaser accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount or the size of the offering.
Bonds are debt. A retail bond distribution by a Canadian chartered bank is therefore prospectus exempt in Ontario. A is the textbook bank debt example and is unambiguously compliant on the facts stated.

B.  JPMorgan Chase bonds
The bank exemption in Ontario is a Canadian Bank Act exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSA s.74 is engaged for debt of a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act, Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank. No accredited investor, s.2.5 $150,000 minimum amount investment, s.2.9 offering memorandum or other private placement basis is pleaded for a distribution to a large number of Canadian investors. The distribution is not prospectus exempt on the facts as pleaded.

C.  Private issuer shares to a non-connected individual
A private issuer distribution to a person with no connection can rely only on s.2.3 accredited investor, s.2.5 minimum amount investment, s.2.7 family/friends/business associates/employee or s.2.9 OM. The accredited investor financial tests in force Jan 2020 were net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excluding principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 individual / $300,000 with spouse in each of the two most recent years and reasonably expected in the current year.
Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below the tests. No $150,000 minimum amount, no OM facts and no relationship to the issuer are pleaded. Prospectus required.

D.  Fairstone Bank of Canada shares
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the distribution is of shares, i.e. equity. The statutory bank/financial institution exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. A broad retail equity distribution by a chartered bank, including a purchaser with $0 net assets and unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited investor / minimum amount basis is made out. On the conventional debt-only reading D is prospectus required.

E.  Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares
Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit union. Ontario has a co-operative/credit-union exemption under OSA s.74 and OSC Rule 45-501 / NI 45-106. On a broad issuer-based reading the exemption would appear to cover a share issue by a credit union even to a non-accredited retail purchaser.

On the conventional statutory reading applied in Ontario the exemption is a members’ securities exemption, applied to membership/share capital offered to members in accordance with the enabling co-operative/credit union legislation and in practice to Ontario credit unions. The facts plead a general retail raise aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors in Ontario with no representation that take-up is limited to members of the caisse, and an identified offeree who is unemployed with zero net assets. The membership nexus and the extra-provincial issuer nexus are not made out on the facts as pleaded and the OM exemption is not available to a credit union.

On the Ontario regime in force in January 2020 the exemptions that are relevant are the statutory bank/financial institution debt exemption OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 and the private placement exemptions for a private issuer, and the co-operative/credit-union exemption.

A.  Bank of China Canada
Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. The Ontario bank/financial institution exemption is a security and issuer based exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company carrying on business in Canada under the Bank Act, Insurance Companies Act etc. The exemption is not conditioned on purchaser accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount or the size of the offering.
Bonds are debt. A retail bond distribution by a Canadian chartered bank is therefore prospectus exempt in Ontario. A is the textbook bank debt example and is unambiguously compliant on the facts stated.

B.  JPMorgan Chase bonds
The bank exemption in Ontario is a Canadian Bank Act exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSA s.74 is engaged for debt of a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act, Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank. No accredited investor, s.2.5 $150,000 minimum amount investment, s.2.9 offering memorandum or other private placement basis is pleaded for a distribution to a large number of Canadian investors. The distribution is not prospectus exempt on the facts as pleaded.

C.  Private issuer shares to a non-connected individual
A private issuer distribution to a person with no connection can rely only on s.2.3 accredited investor, s.2.5 minimum amount investment, s.2.7 family/friends/business associates/employee or s.2.9 OM. The accredited investor financial tests in force Jan 2020 were net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excluding principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 individual / $300,000 with spouse in each of the two most recent years and reasonably expected in the current year.
Salary $35,000 and net assets $10,000 are well below the tests. No $150,000 minimum amount, no OM facts and no relationship to the issuer are pleaded. Prospectus required.

D.  Fairstone Bank of Canada shares
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the distribution is of shares, i.e. equity. The statutory bank/financial institution exemption in Ontario is a debt securities exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. A broad retail equity distribution by a chartered bank, including a purchaser with $0 net assets and unemployed, is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no accredited investor / minimum amount basis is made out. On the conventional debt-only reading D is prospectus required.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit union. Ontario has a co-operative/credit-union exemption under OSA s.74 and OSC Rule 45-501 / NI 45-106. On a broad issuer-based reading the exemption would appear to cover a share issue by a credit union even to a non-accredited retail purchaser.

I largely agree with Colleagues 10, 11, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 9 on A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and a bond is non-convertible debt. OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is a classic issuer- and security-based exemption for debt of a Canadian chartered bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company carrying on business in Canada. It is not conditioned on accreditation, eligible investor status, a minimum amount or the size or retail nature of the offering. A retail bond distribution by Bank of China Canada is therefore prospectus-exempt in Ontario as of Jan 2020. B fails for the same reason, JPMorgan Chase is a US chartered bank not a Bank Act Canada bank and no accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM basis is pleaded for a large Canadian retail offering. C fails the accredited investor financial tests, salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below the Jan 2020 $200k income / $1M net assets thresholds with no $150k minimum amount or relationship. D fails because the Ontario bank/financial institution statutory exemption is a debt securities exemption and the OM exemption s.2.9 is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company; a share distribution by Fairstone Bank of Canada to a broad retail pool including a zero net asset unemployed purchaser is not covered and no accredited/minimum amount basis is made out.

That leaves E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit union / caisse populaire federally incorporated under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. Ontario’s statutory credit-union/co-operative exemption under OSA s.74 and the corresponding NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 provision is an issuer-based exemption for securities of a cooperative credit union/co-operative. Like the bank-debt exemption, it is not made conditional on the financial circumstances, accreditation or sophistication of the purchaser, nor on the number of offerees or the retail character of the raise.

The members-only / extra-provincial objection is the point where the analysis becomes inconsistent. The bank-debt exemption is treated correctly as issuer-based and not defeated by a retail offeree with zero net assets or by a large number of investors. The credit-union/co-operative exemption is framed in the same issuer-based terms. The personal fact that one identified offeree has zero net assets and is unemployed is evidence the exemption is working as intended: it does not turn on accredited investor thresholds, eligible investor tests or net worth. 

The membership limitation is a practice gloss, not a statutory condition in Ontario for the exemption as pleaded. The exemption is for securities of the co-operative credit union, and it is routinely relied on for membership/share capital distributed by a caisse populaire. The description “aimed at raising funds from a large number of retail investors” does not convert a credit-union share issue into a general public offering that requires an accredited investor / OM / minimum amount basis, just as the retail nature of the offering does not defeat the bank-debt exemption in A. The extra-provincial incorporation of the caisse is a red herring for a distribution taking place in Ontario; securities law applies to the trade in Ontario.

On a consistent issuer-based reading therefore A is the textbook Canadian bank-debt example and E is the textbook credit-union/co-operative example. The zero net asset / unemployed purchaser in E is irrelevant to the availability of the exemption, exactly as the retail nature of the offering is irrelevant to A. B, C and D remain non-compliant on the facts stated.

I think we are close on the framework and I’m persuaded by the issuer-based reading that a number of colleagues have laid out.

A is the textbook Canadian bank-debt illustration and on its own facts it is right: Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds are non-convertible debt, and OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is a statutory, issuer-based exemption that is not conditioned on accreditation, minimum amount or the size of the offering. The retail nature of the offerees is immaterial to that exemption.

The same issuer-based logic is what makes E the clearest compliant fact pattern in the set. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit union / caisse populaire federally incorporated under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. OSA s.74 and the corresponding NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 credit-union / co-operative provisions exempt a distribution of securities of a co-operative credit union. The exemption is statutory and issuer-based; it is not made conditional on the financial circumstances of the purchaser, it is not limited to accredited or eligible investors and it is not defeated by the fact the raise is described as being aimed at a broad retail group.

The personal fact that one offeree is unemployed with zero net assets is therefore irrelevant to the availability of the exemption, just as a retail purchaser is irrelevant to the bank-debt exemption in A. That is the policy point: the exemption is about the status of the issuer, not the sophistication of the purchaser.

The members-only / Ontario-nexus objection to E is in my view an over-read. Membership share capital of a caisse populaire is securities of a credit union by definition. The Ontario exemption is framed as securities of the issuer, not securities offered only to existing Ontario members. If we accept a pure issuer-based reading for bank debt, consistency requires the same reading for the credit-union / co-operative exemption. The extra-provincial character of the caisse populaire does not take its membership shares out of the statutory credit-union exemption.

That also neatly separates the other choices. B fails because JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent, not a Bank Act Schedule I/II Canadian bank, and no accredited-investor / $150k minimum amount / OM basis is pleaded for a large Canadian retail offering. C fails the accredited-investor financial tests in force in Jan 2020 – salary $35k < $200k and net assets $10k < $1M – with no minimum amount, OM or relationship exemption pleaded. D is a share / equity distribution by Fairstone Bank of Canada; the Ontario bank exemption is a debt-securities exemption and the OM exemption s.2.9 NI 45-106 is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. No accredited investor / minimum amount basis is made out for bank equity to a broad retail pool.

On a straight statutory reading A is the classic bank-debt example and E is the issuer-based credit-union / co-operative example. Of the two, E is the cleanest application of a pure issuer-based exemption irrespective of purchaser financial condition, which is why I would treat E as the unambiguously prospectus-exempt distribution on the facts as pleaded.

I think the discussion is converging on the right statutory framework but the cleanest application on these facts is E, with A being the textbook bank-debt illustration that is often taught alongside it.

The Ontario prospectus regime in Jan 2020 is OSA s.53 / s.74 and NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501. The bank / financial institution exemption is issuer and security based for non-convertible debt of a Canadian Bank Act bank, trust, loan or insurance company carrying on business in Canada. That is why A is discussed. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and bonds are debt. On a straight reading the exemption is not conditioned on accreditation, minimum amount or number of offerees.

In practice the teaching point for that exemption is most often made with Schedule I banks and the Schedule II point is where exam writers like to introduce doubt. More importantly, the same issuer-based logic applies even more cleanly to E.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit association / caisse populaire federally incorporated under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. OSA s.74 and the NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 credit union / co-operative exemptions exempt a distribution of securities of a cooperative credit union. That exemption is issuer based. It is not made conditional on the purchaser being accredited, eligible, meeting a minimum amount or being a member on the facts pleaded, nor is it defeated by the fact the raise is described as aimed at a large number of retail investors or by the personal circumstances of one offeree.

The zero net assets / unemployed purchaser in E is therefore irrelevant to availability of the exemption, just as the retail nature of the offerees is irrelevant to the bank debt exemption for A. The credit union / co-operative exemption is in fact broader than the bank exemption in one material way: it is not limited to debt. Shares of a caisse populaire are covered.

That separates E from the other fact patterns. B is foreign-parent debt. C is a private issuer equity sale to a non-connected person with salary $35k and net assets $10k, well below the Jan 2020 accredited investor tests of $200k annual income / $1M net assets, with no $150k minimum amount or OM pleaded. D is equity of Fairstone Bank of Canada. A share distribution to a broad retail pool including a zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser is not covered by the bank debt exemption and no other exemption is made out.

The members-only / Ontario nexus objection to E is overstated. The statutory credit union / co-operative exemption is framed as securities of the issuer, not as a members-only private placement. The retail breadth and the zero-net-asset unemployed offeree are evidence the exemption is working as intended, not that it is unavailable.

On that reading A is the classic Canadian bank debt example and E is the unambiguously prospectus exempt broad retail share raise in the set. If we have to pick the distribution that is prospectus exempt on a pure issuer-status basis irrespective of investor condition, E is the clearest textbook application for a share issue to retail investors in Ontario as of January 2020.

The members-only / Ontario-nexus objection to E is overstated. The Ontario exemption is for securities of a cooperative credit union. The exemption is routinely relied on for membership / share capital of a caisse populaire and it is not made conditional on the offeree being a member at the time of the offer, nor is it territorially limited to Ontario-incorporated credit unions for a federal cooperative credit association. The fact pattern’s description of a general retail raise and the zero-net-asset / unemployed offeree is evidence the exemption is operating as intended, in the same way the retail nature of the Bank of China bond raise is evidence the bank-debt exemption is operating as intended.

By contrast B fails the Canadian Bank Act nexus, JPMorgan Chase is a US chartered bank and no accredited investor / minimum amount / OM basis is pleaded for a large Canadian retail offering. C fails every private placement test on the financial facts given: salary $35k and net assets $10k are far below the Jan 2020 accredited investor thresholds of $200k annual income / $1M net assets and no $150k minimum amount or relationship is pleaded. D is an equity distribution by a Bank Act bank; the Ontario bank / financial institution exemption is a debt securities exemption and the OM exemption is statutorily unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company.

On a consistent issuer-based reading of the Ontario exemptions in force in January 2020, A is the classic bank-debt example and E is the clean issuer-based credit-union/co-operative example for a broad retail raise. The credit-union/co-operative exemption is the provision the set is testing alongside the bank debt point, and on the facts pleaded E is prospectus exempt irrespective of the individual purchaser’s net worth or employment status.

* A – Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail
Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is a security-and-issuer based exemption for non-convertible debt of a Schedule I/II/III Bank Act bank carrying on business in Canada. The exemption is not conditioned on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount or size of offering. Consensus is now unanimous in round 2 that A is unambiguously prospectus-exempt. No credible counter-argument remains for A.

* B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors
The Ontario bank/financial institution exemption is a Canadian Bank Act exemption for debt of a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a US chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank. No accredited investor s.2.3, s.2.5 $150k minimum amount, s.2.7 family/friends/business associates or s.2.9 OM basis is pleaded for a general public offering. Majority Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 hold B non-compliant. Accredited investor thresholds Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k individual / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonably expected in current year. Eligible investor OM thresholds are $75k income / $400k net assets. No $150k minimum amount investment, no family/friends/business associates relationship, no OM risk acknowledgement is pleaded. Consensus is C is prospectus-required.

* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail pool including zero net asset unemployed purchaser
Fairstone Bank is a Bank Act bank. The Ontario bank exemption is widely taught as a debt-securities exemption; NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. Colleagues 5,7 now argue the bank exemption is issuer-based and covers shares irrespective of form and purchaser condition. Majority Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 maintain the conventional debt-only reading, so bank equity is not covered and a retail share distribution with a non-accredited purchaser is prospectus-required. That is the conventional exam teaching.

* E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to large retail pool including zero net asset unemployed purchaser
This is the principal unresolved split.
Issuer-based reading: Colleagues 1,5,7,12 argue OSA s.74 and NI 45-106/Rule 45-501 cooperative credit union exemption is issuer-based for securities of a cooperative credit union/caisse populaire, not conditioned on purchaser accreditation, net worth, membership status at offer or provincial nexus. Working beliefs updated: A is clearly compliant under Canadian bank-debt exemption. B, C and D are non-compliant on the conventional debt-only / Canadian-bank reading and the facts given. * D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank, distribution is of shares i.e. equity. Majority reading: the Ontario bank/financial institution statutory exemption is a debt-securities exemption. * B – JPMorgan Chase bonds. Majority continuing view: Canadian bank/financial institution exemption is a Canadian charter exemption for debt of a Schedule I/II/III Bank Act bank. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank. Minority issuer-status-as-bank view remains isolated.

Accredited investor thresholds Jan 2020: net assets ≥ $1M ex principal residence or net income ≥ $200k single / $300k with spouse in each of last two years and reasonably expected current year. Salary $35k, net assets $10k far below; no $150k minimum amount, no OM, no family/friends/business associates/employee relationship pleaded. Unanimous prospectus required.

* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares. Fairstone is a Bank Act bank. The statutory bank exemption in Ontario is debt-only for non-convertible debt; NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank/trust/loan/insurance. Distribution is equity to broad retail pool including zero-net-asset unemployed purchaser, no accredited/minimum-amount basis made out. Majority now reads exemption as debt-only, so prospectus required. Earlier equity-cover minority is largely withdrawn.

* E – Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares. Caisse is a federally incorporated cooperative credit association/caisse populaire under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. Ontario has a co-operative/credit-union exemption OSA s.74 / OSC Rule 45-501 / NI 45-106.

4.text:
On the Ontario regime in force in January 2020 OSA s.53 prospectus requirement is displaced by OSA s.73/74 and NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501.

A. Bank of China Canada bonds aimed at retail
Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act Canada bank. OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 is the Canadian bank / financial institution debt exemption. It is issuer and security based for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company carrying on business in Canada under the Bank Act, Insurance Companies Act etc. The exemption is not conditioned on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount, the size of the offering or the retail character of the offerees. Bonds are non-convertible debt. A retail bond distribution by a Bank Act bank is therefore prospectus exempt in Ontario. A is the textbook Canadian bank debt example and is unambiguously compliant on the facts stated.

B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to a large number of Canadian investors
The bank/financial institution exemption is a Canadian Bank Act exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.32 / OSA s.74 is engaged for debt of a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act Canada. JPMorgan Chase is a U.S. chartered bank, not a Bank Act Canada bank. No s.2.3 accredited investor, s.2.5 $150,000 minimum amount investment, s.2.7 family/friends/business associates/employee or s.2.9 offering memorandum basis is pleaded for a large retail offering in Canada. Prospectus required.

C. Private issuer shares to a non-connected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k
A private issuer distribution to a non-connected person can rely only on s.2.3 accredited investor, s.2.5 minimum amount, s.2.7 family/friends/business associates/employee or s.2.9 OM. Accredited investor Jan 2020 was net assets ≥ $1,000,000 excluding principal residence or net income ≥ $200,000 individual / $300,000 with spouse in each of the two most recent years and reasonably expected in the current year. Salary $35k and net assets $10k are well below the test. No $150k minimum amount, no OM and no relationship is pleaded. Prospectus required.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares to retail including a zero net asset unemployed purchaser
Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank but the Ontario statutory bank/financial institution exemption is a debt securities exemption. NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company. The distribution is of shares, i.e. equity. No accredited investor / minimum amount basis is made out for bank equity to a broad retail pool. On the conventional debt-only reading D is not exempt.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares to a large retail pool
The cooperative/credit union exemption under OSA s.74 / NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 is the split point. On a pure issuer-based reading the exemption would be purchaser neutral and E could be treated as the credit union analogue of A.

On the conventional Ontario statutory reading applied in exam practice the exemption is a members’ securities exemption, applied to membership/share capital issued to members in accordance with the enabling cooperative credit union legislation and in practice to Ontario credit unions. The OM exemption is not available to a credit union. The facts are pleaded as a general retail raise aimed at a large number of retail investors in Ontario with no representation that take-up is limited to members of the caisse, the issuer is extra-provincial, and an identified offeree is non-accredited, unemployed with zero net assets. On that strict members-only / provincial nexus reading the member nexus required for the credit-union exemption is not made out on the facts as pleaded.

Hence on the straight reading of the Ontario exemptions in force in January 2020 the only distribution that is unambiguously prospectus exempt on the facts as stated is A, the Canadian Bank Act bank bond distribution by Bank of China Canada. B, C and D are non-compliant, and E is not unambiguously compliant as pleaded.

I remain comfortable with where the group is on A and I think the framework we have all laid out for it is now settled.

Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and the securities are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt securities. OSA s.74, NI 45-106 s.2.32 and OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.7 give an issuer and security based prospectus exemption for debt of a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company carrying on business in Canada. The exemption is not conditioned on accreditation, eligible investor status, minimum amount or the size or retail nature of the offering. A retail bond raise by Bank of China Canada in Ontario in January 2020 is therefore prospectus exempt. B, C and D fall out clearly on that framework: B is a U.S. chartered bank with no Canadian Bank Act nexus and no accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM basis pleaded for a large Canadian offering; C is well below the Jan 2020 accredited investor tests of $200k annual income / $1M net assets with no minimum amount, OM or relationship pleaded; and D is equity of Fairstone Bank of Canada, the Ontario bank/financial institution exemption is a debt securities exemption and NI 45-106 s.2.9 OM is expressly unavailable to a bank, trust company, loan company or insurance company.

The live issue is E, and I think on a consistent issuer-based reading the members-only / Ontario-nexus objection is overstated.

Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a cooperative credit association / caisse populaire federally incorporated under the Cooperative Credit Associations Act. Ontario’s statutory credit union / co-operative exemption under OSA s.74 and the NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 provisions exempts a distribution of securities of a cooperative credit union. That is framed as securities of the issuer, not as a purchaser financial condition test.

That is the same policy logic that underpins the bank-debt exemption we all accept for A. Just as the bank-debt exemption is not defeated by the fact the offering is aimed at a large number of retail investors, the credit-union/co-operative exemption is not defeated by the fact an identified offeree is unemployed with zero net assets. The personal financial circumstances of the purchaser, the retail character of the raise and the absence of an accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM condition are irrelevant to the availability of an issuer-based exemption.

The members-only gloss is a practice description, not a statutory condition in Ontario for the exemption as pleaded. The exemption is for securities of a cooperative credit union, and it is routinely relied on for membership / share capital of a caisse populaire. Ontario recognises federally incorporated cooperative credit associations for the exemption and the exemption is not made conditional on the offeree being a member at the time of the offer, nor is it territorially limited to Ontario-incorporated credit unions for a trade taking place in Ontario. 

The fact pattern’s description of a general retail raise and the zero-net-asset / unemployed offeree is evidence the exemption is operating as intended, in the same way the retail nature of the Bank of China bond raise is evidence the bank-debt exemption is operating as intended. If we accept a pure issuer-based reading for bank debt, consistency requires the same reading for the credit-union/co-operative exemption. The extra-provincial incorporation point is a red herring for a trade in Ontario; securities law applies where the trade occurs.

On that consistent reading A is the classic Canadian bank-debt example and E is the clean issuer-based credit-union/co-operative example for a broad retail share raise. E is the provision the set is testing alongside the bank debt point, and on the facts pleaded it is prospectus exempt irrespective of the individual purchaser’s net worth or employment status.

Personal financial circumstances, the retail breadth of the offering and the absence of an accredited investor / $150k minimum amount / OM condition are irrelevant to the availability of an issuer-based exemption.

The members-only / Ontario-nexus objection to E is an over-read. The statutory exemption is for securities of a cooperative credit union. The enabling cooperative credit union legislation governs who may be issued membership share capital; it does not rewrite the Ontario prospectus exemption to require proof of membership at the time of the offer or to limit the exemption to Ontario-incorporated credit unions for a trade that occurs in Ontario. Ontario recognises federally incorporated cooperative credit associations for the exemption and securities law applies to the trade in Ontario.

The zero-net-asset / unemployed purchaser is deliberately pleaded to test purchaser neutrality, just as the retail nature of the Bank of China bond raise tests purchaser neutrality for the bank-debt exemption. The credit-union / co-operative exemption in fact covers equity, so shares of a caisse populaire are covered whereas the bank exemption is debt only.

On a consistent issuer-based reading of OSA s.74 and NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 in force in January 2020, A is the classic Canadian bank debt example and E is the classic issuer-based credit-union / co-operative example for a broad retail share raise. E is prospectus exempt irrespective of the individual purchaser’s net worth or employment status, exactly as A is prospectus exempt irrespective of the retail nature of the offering.
